label: Lesson 21
title: Bioelectrochemistry
summary: Living systems run on electron transfer, from respiration to photosynthesis. This lesson looks at how biology and electrochemistry meet: how redox proteins exchange electrons with an electrode, how enzyme electrodes become biosensors, how bacteria can generate current, and how electrochemistry is used to study and stimulate living systems.

intro.text: Biology is full of electrochemistry. Every time a cell respires it moves electrons down a chain of proteins; every nerve impulse is a wave of membrane potential. Bioelectrochemistry studies these processes and, increasingly, wires them to electrodes.

This lesson covers the meeting point: getting an electron from a protein into a metal, turning an enzyme into a selective sensor, harvesting the respiration of bacteria as current, and using electrodes to probe biology.

intro.title: The one-sentence summary
intro.body: Bioelectrochemistry connects biological electron transfer to electrodes, whether the electron comes from a redox protein, an enzyme, or a whole living cell.

sections.title: Electrons and life
sections.summary: Biological energy flows through chains of redox proteins, and cells maintain membrane potentials. The redox sites are usually buried inside proteins, which makes wiring them to an electrode a challenge.
keyPoints: Respiration and photosynthesis move electrons through chains of redox proteins.
Redox centres are usually buried inside the protein, away from the electrode.
Cell membranes maintain a potential difference, the basis of nerve signals.
Electron transfer over distance happens by tunnelling and by hopping between centres.

blocks.text: A cell extracts energy by passing electrons along a chain of proteins, each one handing the electron to the next and releasing a little energy on the way. The same chain, run backwards with light as the input, is photosynthesis. Biology is therefore an electrochemical machine built from proteins.

The difficulty for an electrochemist is that the redox centre - the place where the electron actually sits - is usually buried deep inside the protein, shielded from the outside by the folded chain. An electrode cannot simply touch it. Bridging that distance is the central problem of protein electrochemistry.

The exception is the cell membrane. A living membrane can hold a potential difference across its few-nanometre thickness, and a travelling change in that potential is a nerve impulse. Electrochemistry, and its cousin electrophysiology, grew up studying such potentials.

blocks.title: Why burying the site is useful
blocks.body: By shielding the redox centre, the protein controls exactly who it talks to. That selectivity is what makes biology work, and it is also what makes proteins hard to connect to a macroscopic electrode.

sections.title: Enzyme electrodes
sections.summary: An enzyme can be immobilised on an electrode so that its reaction produces or consumes electrons. The electron may transfer directly or via a mediator, and a mediator often makes the coupling much faster.
keyPoints: An enzyme electrode couples an enzyme's reaction to an electrode.
Direct electron transfer needs the redox site close to the electrode.
A mediator shuttles electrons between the buried site and the electrode.
The enzyme gives selectivity; the electrode gives the measurable signal.

blocks.text: An enzyme electrode immobilises an enzyme on a conducting surface. The enzyme catalyses a reaction, and the electron involved is delivered to or taken from the electrode, so the reaction becomes a current. The enzyme supplies selectivity - only its substrate reacts - and the electrode turns that reaction into a number.

Getting the electron across is the hard part. Direct electron transfer requires the redox site to be near the electrode, which is rarely true for a buried centre. A mediator solves the problem: a small redox molecule shuttles between the enzyme and the electrode, carrying the electron over the distance the protein will not.

The choice between direct and mediated transfer shapes the device. Direct transfer makes a simpler sensor but depends on lucky orientation of the protein. Mediated transfer is more general but adds a reagent and its own electrochemistry to the signal.

blocks.title: Ferrocene and glucose oxidase
blocks.body: Many glucose sensors use a ferrocene derivative as the mediator: it collects electrons from the enzyme's active site and delivers them to the electrode, turning a hidden redox event into a measurable current.

sections.title: Biosensors
sections.summary: A biosensor combines a biological recognition element with an electrochemical transducer. The glucose test strip is the consumer success story, and continuous monitors extend the idea to the body.
keyPoints: A biosensor pairs biological recognition with an electrode signal.
Amperometric biosensors report a current proportional to substrate concentration.
The most successful example is the glucose test strip and its continuous version.
Selectivity comes from the biological element, not from the electrode.

blocks.text: A biosensor has two halves: a biological element that recognises the target, and a transducer, here an electrode, that turns recognition into a signal. The biological half decides what the sensor sees; the electrode half decides how well it can be read.

In an amperometric biosensor the current, often a limiting current, is proportional to the substrate concentration. Because the enzyme is selective, the device can measure glucose in blood without separating the rest of the sample first.

The glucose test strip is the enormous commercial success, tested billions of times a year. Its continuous cousin, an implanted or worn sensor, follows glucose through the day and feeds an insulin pump, closing a loop between measurement and treatment.

blocks.title: Selectivity is the weak point
blocks.body: The electrode will happily react with anything that reaches it, so stray electroactive species - drugs, ascorbate, other metabolites - can confuse the signal. The enzyme's selectivity and a well-chosen operating potential are what keep the sensor honest.

sections.title: Microbial fuel cells
sections.summary: Some bacteria can transfer electrons from their metabolism to an electrode, generating current while consuming organic matter. The promise is wastewater treatment that produces electricity; the problem is low power.
keyPoints: Exoelectrogenic bacteria transfer electrons from their respiration to an electrode.
The electrons come from oxidising organic matter, so the fuel is a waste stream.
Power densities are low but the process also treats the water.
Transfer to the electrode may be direct or use a mediator the bacteria make.

blocks.text: Certain bacteria can breathe onto an electrode. They oxidise organic matter and, instead of delivering the electrons to oxygen, deliver them to a solid anode. The electrode becomes the terminal electron acceptor, and the current it collects is a useful output.

The attraction is that the fuel is free: the organic matter in wastewater is exactly what the bacteria eat. A microbial fuel cell can therefore clean water and generate a little electricity at the same time, which is why it is studied for wastewater treatment.

The catch is power. Electrons cross the bacterium-electrode interface slowly, so the current density is far below that of a chemical fuel cell. Part of the answer is bacteria that grow conductive appendages, or that secrete their own mediators, to improve the transfer.

blocks.title: The double dividend
blocks.body: A microbial fuel cell is judged not only by its watts but by how much pollution it removes. Even a modest power output can be worthwhile if it comes bundled with treatment.

sections.title: Bioelectrochemical systems
sections.summary: The same interface can be turned around: electrodes can drive biological reactions, as in bioelectrosynthesis, or read them, as in DNA and cell sensors. Electrodes also serve to stimulate nerves.
keyPoints: Bioelectrosynthesis uses an electrode to supply electrons to microbes or enzymes to make a product.
DNA and cell sensors use electrochemistry to detect biomolecules.
Nerve stimulation and biosignal recording use the electrode-electrolyte interface for signalling.
The same challenges - selectivity, stability, biocompatibility - recur in every application.

blocks.text: A microbial fuel cell takes electrons out of biology; bioelectrosynthesis pushes them in. Here an electrode supplies electrons to microbes or enzymes that use them to build a wanted product - a fuel or a chemical - from simple feedstocks. The electrode replaces a chemical reducing agent.

Electrochemistry also reads biology. A DNA sensor detects a target sequence through a current that depends on how much of it has hybridised to a probe on the electrode. Cell-based sensors report the metabolic or respiratory activity of living cells.

Finally, the electrode-electrolyte interface is the working surface of electrophysiology: nerve stimulation and the recording of biosignals both rest on it. Across all of these, the same demands return - selectivity, stability and, now, biocompatibility with the living system.

blocks.title: The recurring triangle
blocks.body: Whether the device is a sensor, a fuel cell or a stimulator, it must be selective, stable and compatible with biology. Success in one application rarely transfers automatically to another, because the operating conditions differ.

questions.question: In most redox proteins the site where the electron sits is buried inside the folded protein.
questions.explanation: Burial gives the protein control over whom it reacts with, which is the basis of biological selectivity. It also makes wiring the protein to an electrode difficult.

questions.question: A nerve impulse is best described as:
options: A flow of metal ions along a wire
A travelling change in the potential across a cell membrane
questions.explanation: The membrane holds a potential difference across its few-nanometre thickness, and a travelling change in that potential is the impulse.

questions.question: Respiration moves electrons through a chain of redox proteins.
questions.explanation: Each protein hands the electron to the next, releasing energy along the way. Photosynthesis runs the same kind of chain with light as the input.

questions.question: A mediator in an enzyme electrode is used to:
options: Anchor the enzyme to the electrode
Carry electrons between the buried active site and the electrode
questions.explanation: The redox site is usually buried, so a small redox molecule shuttles the electron between it and the electrode. This makes the coupling general.

questions.question: In an enzyme electrode the enzyme provides selectivity and the electrode provides the measurable signal.
questions.explanation: The enzyme ensures only its substrate reacts, while the electrode turns that reaction into a current or potential. Direct electron transfer needs the site close to the electrode; a mediator bridges the gap when it is not.

questions.question: Which statements about enzyme electrodes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Direct electron transfer needs the redox site near the electrode
A mediator shuttles electrons between the site and the electrode
The enzyme confers selectivity on the sensor
Mediators make the coupling always slower
questions.explanation: Direct transfer needs proximity, mediators bridge the distance, and the enzyme provides selectivity. Mediators usually speed the coupling up rather than slowing it down, which is why they are used.

questions.question: The most commercially successful electrochemical biosensor is:
questions.explanation: The glucose test strip is tested billions of times a year, and its continuous form feeds insulin pumps. Its success comes from combining a selective enzyme with a simple amperometric readout.

questions.question: In a biosensor, selectivity comes from the electrode material rather than the biological element.
questions.explanation: Selectivity comes from the biological recognition element - the enzyme or other bioreceptor. The electrode is the transducer that turns recognition into a current or potential.

questions.question: Stray electroactive species such as ascorbate can interfere with an amperometric biosensor.
questions.explanation: The electrode reacts with anything that reaches it, so interfering species can add to the signal. The enzyme's selectivity and a carefully chosen operating potential limit the problem.

questions.question: In a microbial fuel cell, the electrons come from:
options: Bacteria oxidising organic matter and delivering electrons to the anode
questions.explanation: The bacteria oxidise organic matter, often a waste stream, and pass the electrons to a solid anode. This earns the double dividend of current and water treatment.

questions.question: Microbial fuel cells generate power densities comparable to chemical fuel cells.
questions.explanation: Electron transfer across the bacterium-electrode interface is slow, so power densities are far lower. The attraction is that the fuel is free and the water is treated at the same time.

questions.question: Bioelectrosynthesis uses an electrode to:
options: Supply electrons to microbes or enzymes so they make a product
Measure the temperature of a culture
questions.explanation: Instead of harvesting current, bioelectrosynthesis feeds electrons from the electrode into biology, replacing a chemical reducing agent to build a wanted product.

questions.question: Which demands recur across bioelectrochemical devices? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Selectivity, stability and biocompatibility matter in every application, especially when living cells are involved. Precious-metal use is a concern for some catalysts but is not one of the recurring biological demands.
